Bootstrap Test of Exact Fit for a Structural Equation Model With Complete or Incomplete Data

Source: R/sem_exact_fit_bootstrap.R
sem_exact_fit_bootstrap.Rd

Gives the chi square test of exact fit of a structural equation model a reference distribution that does not assume normal data: the model based bootstrap of Bollen and Stine (1992), in which the data are first transformed so that the model holds in them exactly, as estimated, and the statistic is then recomputed on B samples drawn with replacement from the transformed data. The share of bootstrap statistics at least as large as the observed one is the bootstrap p-value. For incomplete data fitted by full information maximum likelihood (FIML) the transformation is extended so that the FIML estimates of the saturated model on the transformed data are the model implied moments (Enders, 2002; Savalei & Yuan, 2009), and each bootstrap sample keeps the missing values of the rows it draws, so that the model is fitted to it by FIML as it was to the data. Requires lavaan (in Suggests).

Usage

sem_exact_fit_bootstrap(
  fit,
  B = 1000,
  transformation = c("common", "pattern"),
  improper = c("keep", "drop"),
  conf_level = 0.95,
  seed = NULL,
  ncpus = 1L
)

Arguments

fit

A fitted lavaan model: a maximum likelihood fit (estimator ML, MLM, MLMV, or MLR) of raw continuous data, complete or incomplete under missing = "ml" (with auxiliary variables through lavaan's aux or without), in one or several groups, that converged to an admissible solution. See Details for what is refused.

B

Number of bootstrap samples, a single whole number of at least 100. Defaults to 1000: every sample refits the model. A Monte Carlo p-value is run only from a request of at least 100 samples, at which its standard error is at most 0.05; a smaller B is refused before anything is computed (class dmar_count_invalid). See dmar_bootstrap.

transformation

For incomplete data, how the transformation makes the saturated FIML estimates equal the model implied moments: "common" (the default) finds one matrix that transforms every row on its observed variables, symmetric on the scale of the variables divided by their saturated standard deviations, so that the FIML estimating equations hold summed over the missing data patterns; "pattern" transforms the rows of each missing data pattern on their own, with the pattern's own covariance matrix and means, so that each pattern's covariance matrix and means equal the model implied ones exactly, which needs every pattern to have more rows than observed variables. Both are solved on that standardized scale, so the result does not depend on the units of the variables. See Details. Ignored with complete data.

improper

Whether a bootstrap sample whose fit converged to an inadmissible solution counts in the p-value: "keep" (the default) or "drop". A solution is inadmissible when lavaan's post-estimation check finds a negative variance estimate or a covariance matrix that is not positive definite, of the latent variables, of the residuals of the observed variables, or of the residuals of the structural part of the model; with auxiliary variables the check is made on the model's own parameters (see What Is Counted). Either way the row B_improper reports how many there were.

conf_level

Confidence level of the interval for the Monte Carlo error of the bootstrap p-value. Defaults to 0.95.

seed

Random number seed for the bootstrap samples. Defaults to NULL, under which the samples are drawn from, and advance, the current random number stream; supply an integer for a reproducible result, which is set for the call only, the caller's random number state being restored when it returns.

ncpus

The number of processes over which the bootstrap refits are spread. The default 1 runs them in this R session; a larger number uses forked workers or, on Windows, a socket cluster. Every bootstrap sample is drawn before any refit runs, so a given seed gives the same result whatever ncpus is. A session that forks workers and also starts background processes through callr or processx (a Shiny app, a job runner) needs the environment variable PROCESSX_NOTIFY_OLD_SIGCHLD set to a nonempty value before processx is loaded: processx otherwise replaces the signal handler through which parallel learns that a forked worker has finished, and parallel then reports at exit that it could not terminate its workers (processx documents the interaction and the switch). The results are not affected.

Value

A dmar_tbl (class dmar_sem_fit) with columns term and value and, always in this order, the rows chi_square, df, p_chi_square (the asymptotic p-value of the standard statistic), p_bootstrap, p_bootstrap_ci_lower, p_bootstrap_ci_upper, bootstrap_mean, B, B_used, B_improper, B_failed, N, and n_groups. The attributes B, B_used, n_dropped, B_required (100), and bootstrap_status record the samples in the names every bootstrap result of the package carries. The attribute bootstrap is a data frame with one row per bootstrap sample, its chi_square (NA when it was set aside) and its status (proper, improper, not_converged, or error); the attribute transformation records, per group, the transformation applied, the number of missing data patterns, the Newton steps and the largest estimating equation at the solution (on the standardized scale), and the largest difference between the transformed means and the model implied ones; and the sem_fit attribute records the statistic and its degrees of freedom, the transformation requested and the ones applied, the counts, and the lines of the printed footer.

Details

The Model Based Bootstrap

The chi square statistic \(T\) of a maximum likelihood fit follows its chi square distribution under the model only for normal data in large samples. Bollen and Stine (1992) proposed to find its distribution under the model by bootstrap instead: resampling the data as they are would reproduce the misfit of the model as well as the sampling variation, so the data are first transformed to $$Z = (Y - \bar{Y}) S^{-1/2} \hat{\Sigma}^{1/2}$$ (Enders, 2002, Eq. 1), where \(S\) is the sample covariance matrix, \(\hat{\Sigma}\) the covariance matrix the fitted model implies, and the square roots are symmetric. The transformed data have covariance matrix exactly \(\hat{\Sigma}\), so the model fits them exactly, and their distribution otherwise keeps the shape of the data. Each bootstrap sample draws rows of \(Z\) with replacement, within each group as many as the group has (each group is transformed with its own moments), the model is fitted to it, and its statistic \(T^*\) is recorded. The bootstrap p-value is the share of the \(T^*\) at least as large as the observed \(T\) (row p_bootstrap); a small value says that the observed statistic is unusual for data in which the model holds and have this distribution. Under a mean structure the model implied means are added back, so the means hold too. The statistic is the standard (uncorrected) likelihood ratio statistic in every case: the bootstrap replaces the correction a scaled statistic applies, and a fit by MLM or MLR contributes its estimates and its standard statistic. This is the bootstrap lavaan::bootstrapLavaan(type = "bollen.stine") runs for complete data, with the same transformation and resamples: the seed given here, passed to lavaan as its iseed (with lavaan run serially), gives the same \(T^*\). lavaan called without iseed draws its own seed from the caller's random number stream, so a set.seed() before the two calls does not make them agree.

Incomplete Data

With missing values the transformation cannot be applied row by row, since a row observes only some of the variables. Enders (2002, Eq. 4) first extended it by transforming each row with the submatrices, for the variables the row observes, of the saturated and the model implied covariance matrices estimated by FIML from the whole sample, and adding back the model implied means; the model then does not hold exactly in the transformed data, since the rows of a pattern keep their own covariance matrix, and that transformation is not offered here. Savalei and Yuan (2009) gave two transformations under which the FIML estimates of the saturated model on the transformed data are exactly \(\hat{\mu}\) and \(\hat{\Sigma}\), so that the model fits the transformed data exactly under FIML, as the complete data transformation makes it fit exactly under complete data. The "pattern" transformation (their first) transforms the rows of each missing data pattern with the pattern's own covariance matrix and means, so each pattern's rows take exactly the model implied moments of the variables they observe; it needs every pattern to have more rows than observed variables, since the pattern's covariance matrix is inverted, and a pattern that falls short is refused with its index and counts. The "common" transformation (their second, and the default) centers each pattern at its own means, transforms every row with one matrix, symmetric on the standardized scale described below, chosen so that the covariance estimating equations of the saturated FIML model, summed over the patterns, hold at \(\hat{\Sigma}\), and shifts each pattern to \(\hat{\mu}\); it does not need large patterns. DMAR finds the matrix by Newton's method on the standardized variables, starting from the complete data transformation applied to the EM moments, and records the number of steps and the largest estimating equation at the solution in the transformation attribute, where the pattern transformation records the same check computed afresh. Both transformations are solved on the variables divided by their saturated standard deviations, and the transformed values are multiplied back: the matrix of the common transformation and the square roots of the pattern transformation are symmetric on that standardized scale. The bootstrap therefore does not depend on the units of the variables (rescaling an item rescales its transformed values and changes nothing else). Symmetry belongs to the scale on which it is imposed, so the same transformations solved in raw units, as semTools::bsBootMiss() solves the common one (its transformation 2), give transformed data that differ element by element from these and depend on the units; both versions make the saturated FIML estimates exactly \(\hat{\mu}\) and \(\hat{\Sigma}\), so the model holds exactly in either. Each bootstrap sample draws rows of the transformed data with their missing values, so it has the missing data patterns of the data in bootstrap proportions, and the model is fitted to it by FIML. In Enders's (2002) simulation of his transformation, with 10 to 20 percent of the values missing completely at random from nine nonnormal indicators, the bootstrap held the Type I error rate near .05 at \(N\) = 250 and 500, where the uncorrected FIML statistic rejected far too often, and was conservative at \(N\) = 100, the more so the more nonnormal the data and the more missing values; he suggests a sample of about 200 or more with incomplete data. The calibration of the two transformations offered here on the current code is planned, not done.

What Is Counted

A bootstrap sample whose fit did not converge, raised an error, or returned no finite statistic is set aside, and one that converged to an inadmissible solution is counted or set aside as improper says. That includes a sample whose likelihood has no maximum, an error variance running off below zero while the likelihood is flat or still rising (see fa_bifactor): its estimates are wherever lavaan's optimizer stopped on that ridge, but its chi square is not, since the likelihood levels off along the ridge and the optimizer stops only where its steps no longer gain, which puts the statistic within the optimizer's tolerance of its limit. A sample's solution is judged as the fit's is (see What Is Refused); with auxiliary variables that is the check of the model's own parameters, since lavaan's own check would also count as improper the samples in which only the residual covariances of the auxiliary variables are indefinite, which with an auxiliary variable related to a factor can be many samples whose solution is proper. The rows B, B_used, B_improper, and B_failed count them, and a single warning (class dmar_bootstrap_replications_dropped) reports the samples set aside. The p-value is formed from the B_used statistics; when fewer than half of the attempted samples were used, it is NA with a warning of class dmar_bootstrap_insufficient, since a p-value from the samples that happened to converge would describe a selected distribution. The 100 required are held to the number requested, B, and not to B_used: a request that met the count and then had samples set aside still reports its p-value, the warning says how many were used, and the Wilson interval shows the Monte Carlo error from that number. Where refits can fail, request more than the minimum. options(dmar.bootstrap_exploratory = TRUE) lets a smaller B (2 or more) run for a first look or a demonstration; every such call gives a warning of class dmar_bootstrap_exploratory, and the line under the table says so (see dmar_bootstrap). The rows p_bootstrap_ci_lower and p_bootstrap_ci_upper are the Wilson interval for the Monte Carlo error of the p-value at conf_level, the uncertainty that comes from using B_used samples rather than infinitely many (ci_proportion); it is not an interval for anything about the model. The row bootstrap_mean is the mean of the used statistics, the bootstrap estimate of the expected statistic under the model, which the Bollen-Stine adjustments of fit indices use in place of the degrees of freedom.

What Is Refused

A fit is refused when it did not converge (an error of class dmar_not_converged) or has an inadmissible solution (a refusal of class dmar_inadmissible that names the negative variance or the matrix at fault), as for every fit measure of the SEM family (see sem_fit_measures, which explains the check and how it treats auxiliary variables). It is refused with an error of class dmar_exact_fit_bootstrap_scope, whose reason element names the case (see dmar_metadata), when it was made from summary statistics rather than raw data (there are no rows to transform); when it has ordered indicators or was fitted by an estimator other than maximum likelihood (the transformation is derived for the normal theory fit function); when it is a two-level model, has a cluster variable (the resamples draw rows independently, which the refit could not undo) or sampling weights, uses two-stage estimation (whose statistic is not the likelihood ratio statistic the bootstrap refits), or conditions on observed exogenous variables (fixed.x = TRUE with such variables, or conditional.x = TRUE: the transformation moves every variable, and the conditional likelihood holds some fixed; refit with fixed.x = FALSE, and with conditional.x = FALSE too, since lavaan does not take the first beside conditional.x = TRUE); and when its analysis data keep missing values without FIML (as under pairwise deletion) or it has no standard test statistic. A missing data pattern with no more rows than observed variables is refused for the pattern transformation with an error of class dmar_pattern_too_small, which carries the pattern, its counts, and its group, and a transformation that is undefined for the data (a moment that is not positive definite, a Newton iteration that does not converge) with one of class dmar_transformation_undefined. These three classes, and dmar_inadmissible, inherit dmar_refusal; dmar_not_converged is caught by its own name. The checks of B, conf_level, and ncpus are argument checks and give plain errors. A fit whose cases were removed by listwise deletion is bootstrapped on its complete cases, as it was fitted, with a warning. A fit by MLM, MLMV, or MLR is accepted: its estimates are the ML estimates, and the bootstrap refits and resamples its standard statistic.

References

Bollen, K. A., & Stine, R. A. (1992). Bootstrapping goodness-of-fit measures in structural equation models. Sociological Methods & Research, 21(2), 205–229. doi:10.1177/0049124192021002004

Enders, C. K. (2002). Applying the Bollen-Stine bootstrap for goodness-of-fit measures to structural equation models with missing data. Multivariate Behavioral Research, 37(3), 359–377. doi:10.1207/S15327906MBR3703_3

Savalei, V., & Yuan, K.-H. (2009). On the model-based bootstrap with missing data: Obtaining a p-value for a test of exact fit. Multivariate Behavioral Research, 44(6), 741–763. doi:10.1080/00273170903333590

See also

sem_fit_measures for the asymptotic test of exact fit beside the other fit measures, and equivalence_rmsea for the test of not close fit.

Examples

# Two correlated factors for six of the holzinger_swineford tests, with
# the cube and sentence scores of about a third of the students missing
# at random given the general information score, which the FIML fit
# takes as an auxiliary variable. lavaan notes that it adds the
# auxiliary variable and warns that the residual covariance matrix,
# which includes it, is not positive definite; the model's own solution
# is proper (see What Is Refused). B = 10 keeps the example quick and
# is below the 100 a reported p-value needs; the option lets it run
# and the warning says so. Use the default of 1000 or more in an
# analysis.
d <- holzinger_swineford[c("t1_visual_perception", "t2_cubes", "t4_lozenges",
                           "t6_paragraph_comprehension", "t7_sentence",
                           "t9_word_meaning", "t5_general_information")]
set.seed(113)
drop <- runif(nrow(d)) < plogis((d$t5_general_information - 30) / 10) - 0.35
d[drop, c("t2_cubes", "t7_sentence")] <- NA
fit <- lavaan::cfa(
  "visual  =~ t1_visual_perception + t2_cubes + t4_lozenges
   textual =~ t6_paragraph_comprehension + t7_sentence + t9_word_meaning",
  data = d, missing = "ml", std.lv = TRUE, aux = "t5_general_information")
#> lavaan NOTE:  
#>    auxiliary (aux) variable(s) added to the model as saturated correlates 
#>    (estimated with FIML and hidden from the output): t5_general_information
#> Warning: lavaan->lav_object_post_check():  
#>    the covariance matrix of the residuals of the observed variables (theta) 
#>    is not positive definite; use lavInspect(fit, "theta") to investigate.
old <- options(dmar.bootstrap_exploratory = TRUE)
sem_exact_fit_bootstrap(fit, B = 10, seed = 113)
#> Warning: sem_exact_fit_bootstrap(): B = 10 is below the 100 replications a Monte Carlo p-value is reported from (100 for a Monte Carlo p-value). The p-value is shown because options(dmar.bootstrap_exploratory = TRUE) is set. With 10 replications it will move from seed to seed; use the result to explore or to demonstrate, and report a p-value only from B of at least 100. B, B_used, and B_required are recorded in the result.
#>  term                 value   
#>  chi_square           23.859  
#>  df                   8       
#>  p_chi_square         0.0024  
#>  p_bootstrap          < 0.0001
#>  p_bootstrap_ci_lower 0.0000  
#>  p_bootstrap_ci_upper 0.2775  
#>  bootstrap_mean       6.604   
#>  B                    10      
#>  B_used               10      
#>  B_improper           0       
#>  B_failed             0       
#>  N                    301     
#>  n_groups             1       
#> 
#> Confidence level: 95%
#> 
#> Transformation: incomplete data, one matrix for every pattern (Savalei & Yuan, 2009); the statistic is the standard likelihood ratio statistic under FIML
#> Bootstrap: B = 10 samples, 10 used; p_bootstrap is the share of used statistics at least the observed one, with the Wilson interval for its Monte Carlo error at 95 percent. Exploratory: below the 100 samples a reported p-value needs
#> Sample size: N = 301 in 1 group
options(old)
